title: Don Quixote, pages 1–12
sub: Chapter I — An Old-School Gentleman Gone Mad. Twenty questions, about ten minutes, all of it straight from the pages you read.
cite: Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes, Core Classics abridged for young readers
note: Read the question, then pick. Get one wrong and you can take a hint, which tells you the page to look at. Nothing here comes from any other version of the story.

items.q: Where does the gentleman live?
opts: In a village in the province of La Mancha, in Spain
In the city of Seville, on the southern coast of Spain
In a castle in the mountains above a village in Spain
On a farm in the hills of Portugal, close to the border
items.hint: The very first sentence names the province. He keeps an ancient lance and shield hung up in his hall there.
items.why: “Once upon a time there lived in a village in Spain, in the province of La Mancha.” Later he puts that name into his own.

items.q: What was his name at the start of the story, before he changed it?
opts: Amadis
Rocinante
Quixania
Caraculiambro
items.hint: One short sentence gives it, right after the book says he was about fifty and a great lover of hunting.
items.why: “His name was Quixania.” He invents Don Quixote for himself later on.

items.q: What was he like at the beginning of the story?
opts: A wealthy young lord with a large household of servants, horses and dogs
About fifty, thin but tough, an early riser and a great lover of hunting
A young and strong man who had already been trained as a knight
A soldier who had fought in many real battles for the king
items.hint: He was thin, with a lean face, and he was a very early riser.
items.why: “Our gentleman was about fifty, thin, but tough of body, with a lean face, a very early riser, and a great lover of hunting.”

items.q: The book explains the word chivalry in a grey circle. What does it mean?
opts: The armor, weapons and horses that a knight owned and looked after
The ceremony in which a young man was made a knight by his lord
The ideals of medieval knights — gallantry, honor and courtesy
A long journey taken on horseback in search of adventure and fame
items.hint: It is about how knights behaved, especially toward women. The stories about them were called romances.
items.why: “The ideals of medieval knights that emphasized gallantry, honor and courtesy, especially toward women.”

items.q: What did he sell so that he could buy more books?
opts: His best suit of clothes for Sundays and holidays
The ancient lance and shield from his hall
His hunting dog and his riding horse
Several acres of good cropland
items.hint: He gave up part of the very land his income came from, to buy as many books as he could lay his hands on.
items.why: “He even sold several acres of good cropland in order to buy as many books about chivalry as he could.”

items.q: What did all that reading finally do to him?
opts: It made him a better hunter than he had ever been before
His brain became agitated and his judgment warped
It made him want to write a book of romances of his own
It made him famous among the gentlemen of his village
items.hint: He lost interest in hunting and neglected his daily concerns. The book says what happened to his judgment.
items.why: “His brain became so agitated and his judgment so warped, that he resolved to become a knight himself.”

items.q: What did he decide to become?
opts: A writer of romances about knights and their adventures
A soldier in the king's army, fighting in real battles
A knight, riding about the world setting wrongs right
A farmer with far more cropland than he had before
items.hint: He wanted to do what the men in his books did, and go out seeking adventures.
items.why: He resolved “to become a knight himself and ride about the world setting wrongs right and seeking adventures.”

items.q: When he polished up his ancestors' old armor, what was missing?
opts: A sword, so he had to borrow one from a neighbor
A shield, which had been lost many years before
Gloves, without which he could not hold his lance
A helmet — he had only a simple steel cap
items.hint: One piece only half did the job, so he invented the rest of it himself out of cardboard.
items.why: “There was no helmet, only a simple steel cap,” so he made a visor to go with it.

items.q: What happened when he tested his new cardboard visor?
opts: His sword broke in half against the hard cardboard
He destroyed it with one stroke of his sword
It held up perfectly well and he was delighted
He decided it was too risky and did not test it
items.hint: He wanted to know whether it would resist cuts, so he drew his sword and struck it.
items.why: “He made a stroke at it and in one instant demolished” the work of a whole week.

items.q: What did he name his horse, and how long did it take him to decide?
opts: Bucephalus, after a single day
Rocinante, after four days
Dulcinea, after eight whole days
Amadis, after a whole week
items.hint: The animal was only skin and bone, but he thought it finer than the famous horse of Alexander.
items.why: “He spent four days considering” the matter and “at last fixed on Rocinante.”

items.q: What name did he finally give himself?
opts: Don Belianis of the Steel Cap
Don Quixote de la Mancha
Don Quixote of Toboso
Don Amadis of Gaul and Spain
items.hint: It took him eight days more. He copied the valiant Amadis, who added the name of his country to his own.
items.why: He enlarged it to Don Quixote de la Mancha, so he “made clear his origin and honored his country.”

items.q: Who was the lady he called Dulcinea del Toboso?
opts: A princess he had once met at the court of the king of Spain
A good-looking farmer's daughter named Aldonza Lorenzo
A lady who had written to him about the books he loved
His niece, who was under twenty and lived in his house
items.hint: She lived in his own neighborhood, and she did not seem to know or care anything about him.
items.why: Aldonza Lorenzo. He renamed her Dulcinea del Toboso because she was a native of Toboso.

items.q: When did he set out on his first journey?
opts: At noon in the middle of a cold winter, with snow on the ground
One morning before daybreak, on one of the hottest days in July
On a cool evening in spring, just as the sun was going down
At midnight, during one of the worst storms of the year
items.hint: He went out through a private gate of his yard, so that nobody would see him leave.
items.why: “One morning before daybreak, on one of the hottest days in July, he donned his armor, mounted Rocinante.”

items.q: Which road did Don Quixote take?
opts: The widest and busiest road that he could find
The road leading back toward his own village
The road that led south in the direction of Seville
Whichever road his horse chose
items.hint: He thought that letting it happen this way was the true spirit of adventure.
items.why: “He allowed his horse to follow whatever road it pleased, considering this to be the true spirit of adventure.”

items.q: He reached an inn just before nightfall. What did he think it was?
opts: A monastery where the monks would give him food and a bed for the night
A castle with four towers, silver spires, a drawbridge and a moat
A shepherd's hut of the kind he had been looking for all day
The great stone house of a giant he would have to fight
items.hint: Everything he saw was changed by his books. He waited at the door for a dwarf or a page to announce him.
items.why: He “at once pictured this inn as a castle with four towers, spires of polished silver, a drawbridge and moat.”

items.q: A pig-driver blew his horn to call his herd. What did Don Quixote think it was?
opts: A warning that robbers were somewhere near
A bell calling the guests in to their supper
A trumpet announcing his arrival
A church bell ringing in a village nearby
items.hint: He had been waiting at the door of what he thought was a castle, expecting exactly this from the battlements.
items.why: “At once Don Quixote recognized this as the signal of his arrival,” and approached the ladies with great self-satisfaction.

items.q: Why did the innkeeper agree to make Don Quixote a knight?
opts: He was frightened of what the madman might do to him
He had been a knight himself when he was a young man
He hoped to be paid a great deal of money for doing it
He wanted to amuse himself and his guests
items.hint: He worked out straight away what kind of madness his guest had, and he knew the romances of knights-errant well.
items.why: The host “could not resist the chance to play along with the folly of Don Quixote in order to amuse himself and his guests.”

items.q: Don Quixote wanted to lay his armor before the altar in the chapel. Why did he not?
opts: There was no chapel anywhere near the inn, and never had been
The chapel had been demolished so that it could be rebuilt
The innkeeper told him that knights never really did that
He changed his mind and chose the stable instead
items.hint: The host had an answer ready, and said such a thing was allowed in cases of necessity.
items.why: The chapel “had recently been demolished so that it might be rebuilt,” so he put his armor in a trough in the yard.

items.q: What happened when a mule driver came to move the armor out of the trough?
opts: Don Quixote politely asked him to leave it alone
The innkeeper came out and sent the driver away
Don Quixote was asleep and did not notice him
Don Quixote knocked him out with his lance
items.hint: The driver only wanted to fetch water for his mules. A second one came along later and got exactly the same.
items.why: “The vigilant Don Quixote gave him such a thwack on the head with his lance that he was knocked out.”

items.q: The last page of tonight's reading is a full-page picture. What does it show?
opts: Don Quixote fighting off the angry mule drivers with his shield
Don Quixote kneeling as the innkeeper dubs him a knight
Don Quixote marching up and down in the bright moonlight
Don Quixote riding away from the inn at first light
items.hint: Look at the caption printed under the picture. He is guarding something, all night long.
items.why: The caption reads: “For hours he marched up and down in the bright moonlight.” He is watching his armor.
